title: The Morning Brief: 14 verified stories from the desk, in brief
dek: A digest edition: the desk's verified and published stories from the last 36 hours, each in a sentence or two, newest first.
author: GoCheckMyNews
key_fact: Surveillance footage contradicted Castro's sworn account that Sosa-Celis attacked him before the shooting.
bottom_line: Castro faces six counts in federal court for the false statements charge while Minnesota pursues state assault and false reporting charges. The outcome of the separate civil rights investigation and the administration's reasoning for prioritizing false statement charges over civil rights violations remain unresolved.
body: ICE Officer Charged With False Statements in January Shooting of Venezuelan Immigrant. A federal grand jury indicted ICE officer Christian Castro on Wednesday, September 3, for making false statements to the FBI about a January 14 shooting in Minneapolis. Castro shot Venezuelan immigrant Julio Cesar Sosa-Celis through a closed door; surveillance footage contradicted Castro's claim that Sosa-Celis attacked him.

Missouri Supreme Court blocks GOP-drawn congressional map from November elections. The Missouri Supreme Court ruled Thursday that the state's new GOP-drawn congressional redistricting map cannot be used in November 2026 elections. Instead, voters will decide the map's fate via a ballot referendum on November 5, and the November election will proceed under the previous district lines, preserving a Democratic-held seat.

Suspect in Downtown Minneapolis Mass Shooting Was Facing Eviction. Carlton Neal Johnson, 35, is believed responsible for a mass shooting Wednesday at a downtown Minneapolis apartment complex that killed two residents and injured six others, including three police officers. Court documents show Johnson faced eviction after multiple incidents including assault allegations, openly displaying a firearm to management, and brandishing the weapon to residents over a two-week period in June.

Trump Administration Misses Own Deadline for Federal Citizenship Lists Portal. The Trump administration announced it will miss its own September 4 deadline to publish state-by-state citizenship lists on a federal portal. Instead of meeting the 60-day-before-Election requirement, the Justice Department told courts it would give 48 hours notice before launching. Multiple lawsuits challenge the accuracy and legality of the data-sharing plan.

Two workers rescued alive from Nepal hydropower tunnel, nine days after devastating flood. Two construction workers were pulled alive from the Trishuli-3A hydropower tunnel in Nepal on September 4, nine days after an August 26 flood killed over 1,200 people across Nepal and Tibet. The rescue raised hope that more of the hundreds still missing in hydropower tunnels could be found alive.

Coast Guard aircraft carrying DHS Secretary Mullin loses engine, lands safely at Reagan National. A 25-year-old Coast Guard twin-engine aircraft carrying Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin lost its right engine on Wednesday afternoon and made an emergency landing at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport. All 14 people aboard, including the secretary, were unharmed.

Democrats demand DHS release $39.6 million in election security funds with midterms two months away. Senators Alex Padilla and Rep. Joseph Morelle have called on Homeland Security to restore over $39.6 million in congressionally appropriated election security funds, citing cuts that left the Election Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center unable to provide free services to state and local election offices. The lawmakers cited concerns about foreign interference and cyberattacks as the midterm election approaches.

Federal judge blocks Trump's latest order limiting birthright citizenship (September 2, 2026). U.S. District Judge Deborah Boardman blocked President Trump's August 6, 2026 executive order limiting birthright citizenship on September 2, ruling it unconstitutional under the 14th Amendment. The ruling marks the second judicial block of a Trump birthright citizenship order in a year.

Federal judge weighs extending ban on USPS mail ballot rule, 70 days before midterms. U.S. District Court Judge Indira Talwani is deciding whether to extend a block on Trump administration mail ballot regulations affecting millions of voters. The judge stated she has no details on how the Postal Service will implement the rule, and the temporary ban expires next week as states begin mailing ballots. The administration has signaled it will appeal to the Supreme Court.

Gloria Steinem, pioneering feminist journalist, dies at 92. Gloria Steinem, who transformed American journalism and led the modern women's movement for seven decades, died on September 3, 2026, at her home in New York City. Her career spanned from undercover reporting on workplace sexism to founding Ms. magazine and co-founding the National Women's Political Caucus.

House passes Israel boycott penalties bill, 237-169. The House passed the Protect Economic and Academic Freedom Act on September 3 by a 237-169 vote, requiring federally funded universities to certify they do not boycott Israel or restrict students from participating in Israeli programs. Thirty-three Democrats joined Republicans; two Republicans opposed. The bill now heads to the Senate.

House rejects constitutional amendment to lock Supreme Court at nine justices, September 2, 2026. The House voted 212-206 on September 2, 2026 to reject a proposed constitutional amendment that would permanently fix the Supreme Court at nine justices. The vote fell short of the two-thirds majority required to advance. All but one Democrat voted against the amendment, while one Democrat, Rep. Don Davis of North Carolina, voted in favor.

Jury deadlocked in Lindsay Clancy trial after six days of deliberation. The jury in the Lindsay Clancy murder trial became deadlocked after six days and more than 28 hours of deliberations. Clancy is charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children. The judge applied a final 'dynamite' instruction Wednesday to attempt to break the impasse; jurors are scheduled to return Friday.

Leon Black sues to block House subpoenas on Epstein payments; skips deposition on September 3. Private equity investor Leon Black filed a federal lawsuit Thursday to block House Oversight Committee subpoenas demanding testimony and documents about his financial relationship with Jeffrey Epstein, and failed to appear for a scheduled deposition the same day. Black has paid Epstein between $158 million and $180 million, according to different sources, and faces potential contempt of Congress proceedings.
